sections.h2: Does New Jersey have a homestead exemption?
sections.html:
People searching for a New Jersey homestead exemption usually end up at the state's property tax relief programs. The Division of Taxation runs three of them for homeowners: Senior Freeze (Property Tax Reimbursement), ANCHOR and Stay NJ, all filed on one combined application called the PAS-1. Municipalities add their own deductions on top.

The programs pay benefits to qualifying owners and are tied to a principal residence and to income. The state's own FAQ says eligibility rules, income limits and benefit amounts for each program depend on appropriation in the State Budget, so they can shift from year to year.

The application for 2025 closed on November 2, 2026, per the Division of Taxation. Anyone who missed it should look at what the next filing season brings on the Division's relief page.

sections.h2: Which New Jersey property tax relief program fits which homeowner?
sections.html:
The three programs overlap, and the Division decides which benefits an applicant gets. The table compares them using the Division's published rules.

NJ Division of Taxation property tax relief programs, 2025 application year
ProgramWho qualifiesIncome limit
ANCHORHomeowners who owned and occupied the home on October 1, 2025, and renters$250,000 for homeowners, $150,000 for renters
Senior FreezeAge 65 or older, or receiving Social Security or Railroad Retirement disability, and owned and lived in the home since December 31, 2022 or earlier$172,475 for 2025
Stay NJHomeowners 65 or older who owned and lived in the home all 12 months of 2025$200,000 or less

A homeowner under 65 who does not receive Social Security disability can only qualify for ANCHOR, according to the FAQ. A homeowner who is 65 or older may qualify for all three.

sections.h2: How much does Stay NJ pay?
sections.html:
The Division's Stay NJ page ties the maximum to income. For the 2027 payments covering the 2025 tax year, the maximum benefit is $6,500 at income up to $100,000, $5,000 above that through $150,000, and $4,000 above that through $200,000. Over $200,000 the benefit is zero.

Payments come in quarterly installments. The Division says the 2025 benefit is paid in February and May of 2027, and the remainder of the earlier 2024 benefit was split between August and November 2026. Each applicant gets a benefit statement that lists Senior Freeze, ANCHOR and Stay NJ amounts.

The FAQ sets one cap that applies to all three: total relief cannot exceed the property taxes paid on the principal residence for the qualifying year. Property tax relief payments are not taxable income for New Jersey state taxes.

sections.h2: What property and ownership rules apply?
sections.html:
The home must be the applicant's principal residence. The FAQ defines that as the place you live most of the time and where you vote or get mail, and for owners it is the property on the deed or tax records. A vacation home, a second home or a rental property does not qualify.

  • Senior Freeze: not available on property with more than four units, or with four units or fewer that contains more than one commercial unit, and not available if you make P.I.L.O.T. payments instead of property tax.
  • Stay NJ: mobile homeowners and renters are excluded, a co-owned home is calculated on your ownership percentage, and a duplex is calculated on the share of the property you occupy.
  • Trusts and life estates: a trust beneficiary, or someone with a life estate or a 99-year lease, can qualify and must send the trust, deed or lease document.

Condominium owners and resident co-op shareholders who pay property tax on their unit count as homeowners, the relief page says.

sections.h2: What local New Jersey property tax deductions exist?
sections.html:
Municipalities handle several deductions and exemptions directly. The Division of Taxation lists a $250 deduction for senior citizens and disabled persons, a $250 veteran deduction, and a 100 percent exemption for disabled veterans.

The senior and disabled deduction has its own tests in the Division's brochure. The owner must be 65 or older, or permanently and totally disabled, or an unmarried surviving spouse age 55 or older of such a person. The owner must have lived in New Jersey for a year as of October 1 before the deduction year, owned and lived in the dwelling on that date, and kept income to $10,000 or less with certain exclusions such as Social Security. Form PTD is filed with the municipal assessor or collector, followed by a yearly income statement.

For the veteran programs and the exact forms, ask the local tax assessor. These deductions come through the town, not through the state application.

sections.h2: What happens to relief benefits if I sell or move?
sections.html:
The ANCHOR FAQ says a homeowner who moved during the year is still eligible, but the benefit follows the qualifying property owned and occupied on October 1. A divorced or separated applicant follows the same test: whoever owned and occupied the home on October 1 may apply.

The Division's older seller guide covers the closing side. It says that when a benefit check is processed after a move has been properly shown on the application, the money goes to the seller. If the move is not shown, the seller needs to take credit for the benefit at closing, and if the seller, an attorney or the closing agent misses it, the credit lands on the new owners' taxes. That guide describes the Homestead Benefit, the earlier program, so ask the title company how current benefits are being handled for your closing.

Senior Freeze recipients who buy another New Jersey home must re-establish eligibility for the new property. The guide says a seller who received a reimbursement the year before moving waits two years for a new base year instead of the standard three, then files Form PTR-1-C.

sections.h2: What other tax breaks matter when selling a New Jersey home?
sections.html:
The same Division guide lists the main items a New Jersey seller meets at closing. Sales tax is not due on a home sale, and the seller pays the state Realty Transfer Fee of 1 percent under the guide's summary. Every seller furnishes a GIT/REP form to record the deed, and New Jersey residents use GIT/REP-3 to avoid an estimated income tax payment at closing.

A seller who qualifies for the federal principal residence exclusion can exclude up to $250,000 of gain, or $500,000 on a joint return, after owning and living in the home two of the last five years. Nonresident sellers face an estimated payment of 2 percent of the sale price or 8.97 percent of net gain unless an exemption applies.

The Division's realty fee page shows the transfer fee is figured per $500 of consideration, with rates that step up as the price rises and an extra Graduated Percent Fee on residential sales above $1,000,000.

faqs.q: Is there a New Jersey homestead exemption that lowers my assessed value?
faqs.a: No single program works that way. New Jersey offers ANCHOR, Senior Freeze and Stay NJ as payments through the state, plus local deductions such as the $250 senior and disabled deduction handled by your municipality.

faqs.q: Who qualifies for ANCHOR as a homeowner?
faqs.a: A New Jersey resident who owned and lived in the home on October 1, 2025, with gross income up to $250,000. Renters qualify with income up to $150,000. The home must be the principal residence.

faqs.q: Can I get Stay NJ if I am under 65?
faqs.a: No. The Division says you or your spouse must have been 65 or older in 2025, and receiving Social Security disability does not change that. Mobile homeowners and renters are also excluded.

faqs.q: What if I sold my house after filing the property tax relief application?
faqs.a: The benefit follows the home you owned and occupied on October 1. Show the move on the application, or take credit at closing as the state's seller guide describes, so the benefit does not pass to the new owners.

faqs.q: Do property tax relief payments count as taxable income in New Jersey?
faqs.a: No. The Division of Taxation FAQ says relief payments are not taxable income for New Jersey state taxes. Each applicant's total benefits also cannot exceed the property taxes paid on the home.
